sections.title: BJT Structure
sections.summary: Three doped regions (emitter, base, collector) form two pn junctions. Two types: npn and pnp. The base is thin and lightly doped; emitter is heavily doped.

sections.title: Basic BJT Operation
sections.summary: Forward-reverse bias: BE junction forward-biased, BC junction reverse-biased. IE = IC + IB. Most emitter electrons diffuse through the thin base into the collector.

sections.title: Characteristics & Parameters
sections.summary: βDC = IC/IB (current gain, also called hFE). αDC = IC/IE. VBE ≈ 0.7 V. Collector curves show saturation, active, and breakdown regions. DC load line connects cutoff (VCE = VCC) to saturation (IC(sat)).

sections.title: BJT as Amplifier
sections.summary: Voltage gain Av = RC/r'e. The transistor amplifies because a small ac base voltage produces a large ac collector voltage. DC uses uppercase subscripts; ac uses lowercase.

sections.title: BJT as Switch
sections.summary: Cutoff: IB = 0, VCE = VCC (open switch). Saturation: IC = (VCC − VCE(sat))/RC (closed switch). IB(min) = IC(sat)/βDC.

sections.title: Phototransistor
sections.summary: Base current generated by light (Iλ). IC = βDC·Iλ. Dark current ICEO in nA range. Used in optocouplers (LED + phototransistor) with CTR parameter.

sections.title: Categories & Packaging
sections.summary: Three broad categories: general-purpose/small-signal, power, and RF. Packages include DIP, SO, TO-92, TO-220, TO-3, etc.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.summary: Test BJT as two diodes with DMM. Open junction reads OL. Common faults: open base resistor → cutoff; open collector → no IC; shorted junctions.

questions.text: A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals.
questions.explanation: The three terminals of a BJT are the base, emitter, and collector.

questions.text: The three regions of a BJT are base, emitter, and cathode.
questions.explanation: The three regions are base, emitter, and collector — not cathode. 'Cathode' is a diode terminal.

questions.text: For operation in the linear or active region, the base-emitter junction of a transistor is forward-biased.
questions.explanation: Active (linear) region requires BE junction forward-biased and BC junction reverse-biased (forward-reverse bias).

questions.text: Two types of BJT are npn and pnp.
questions.explanation: npn has two n regions separated by a p base; pnp has two p regions separated by an n base.

questions.text: The base current and collector current are approximately equal.
questions.explanation: IB is much smaller than IC. The collector current is βDC times the base current (IC = βDC·IB).

questions.text: The dc voltage gain of a transistor is designated βDC.
questions.explanation: βDC is the dc current gain (IC/IB), not voltage gain. Voltage gain is Av = RC/r'e.

questions.text: Cutoff and saturation are the two normal states of a linear transistor amplifier.
questions.explanation: A linear amplifier operates in the active (linear) region. Cutoff and saturation are the two states of a transistor switch.

questions.text: When a transistor is saturated, the collector current is maximum.
questions.explanation: In saturation, IC has reached its maximum value IC(sat) = (VCC − VCE(sat))/RC and cannot increase further.

questions.text: βDC and hFE are two different transistor parameters.
questions.explanation: They are the same parameter — both represent dc current gain (IC/IB). hFE is just the datasheet designation for βDC.

questions.text: Voltage gain of a transistor amplifier depends on the collector resistor and the internal ac resistance.
questions.explanation: Av = RC/r'e, so voltage gain depends on the collector resistance RC and the internal ac emitter resistance r'e.

questions.text: Amplification is the output voltage divided by the input current.
questions.explanation: Voltage amplification (gain) is output voltage divided by input voltage: Av = Vout/Vin. Dividing voltage by current gives impedance, not gain.

questions.text: A transistor in cutoff acts as an open switch.
questions.explanation: In cutoff, IB = 0, IC ≈ 0, and VCE = VCC — the transistor behaves like an open switch between collector and emitter.

questions.text: The three terminals of a bipolar junction transistor are called
questions.explanation: The three terminals are base (B), emitter (E), and collector (C).

questions.text: In a pnp transistor, the p regions are
questions.explanation: In a pnp transistor the two outer regions are p-type: the emitter and the collector. The base is n-type.

questions.text: For operation as an amplifier, the base of an npn transistor must be
options: positive with respect to the emitter
negative with respect to the emitter
positive with respect to the collector
questions.explanation: The BE junction must be forward-biased, so the base must be positive relative to the emitter (for npn).

questions.explanation: βDC = IC/IB, which is the dc current gain of the transistor.

questions.explanation: βDC = IC/IB = 50IB/IB = 50.

questions.explanation: A forward-biased silicon pn junction has approximately 0.7 V across it.

questions.text: The bias condition for a transistor to be used as a linear amplifier is called
questions.explanation: Forward-reverse bias means BE junction forward-biased and BC junction reverse-biased — the active region for linear amplification.

questions.text: If the output of a transistor amplifier is 5 V rms and the input is 100 mV rms, the voltage gain is
questions.explanation: Av = Vout/Vin = 5 V / 0.1 V = 50.

questions.explanation: Lowercase r′ with a subscript (like r′e) designates an internal ac resistance of the transistor.

questions.explanation: In saturation VCE drops to VCE(sat), typically a few tenths of a volt — its minimum value.

questions.text: To saturate a BJT,
options: VCC must be at least 10 V
questions.explanation: Saturation requires enough base current so that IC reaches IC(sat). The minimum IB needed is IC(sat)/βDC, so IB must exceed this.

questions.text: Once in saturation, a further increase in base current will
options: cause the collector current to increase
cause the collector current to decrease
questions.explanation: Once saturated, IC is at maximum. More IB cannot push IC higher — the relationship IC = βDC·IB no longer holds.

questions.explanation: In a phototransistor, incident light generates the base current (Iλ), which is directly proportional to light intensity.

questions.explanation: Just like a regular BJT, IC = βDC times the base current. For a phototransistor, that base current is the light-generated Iλ.
